title: Space Packet Protocols
organisation: Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS)
status_notes: Original issue (Document Control table, PDF p. 6). The Report is explicitly not part of the Space Packet Protocol or Encapsulation Packet Protocol Recommended Standards; if it conflicts with them, the Recommended Standards prevail (1.2, PDF p. 8).
summary:
A short CCSDS Green Book that explains, from the user's point of view, the two CCSDS packet protocols: the [Space Packet Protocol](../ccsds/space-packet.md) (SPP, [133.0-B-2](ccsds-133-0-133x0b2e2.md)) and the [Encapsulation Packet Protocol](../ccsds/encapsulation.md) (EPP, [133.1-B-3](ccsds-133-1-133x1b3e1.md)). It specifies nothing itself; it gives the concepts, the rationale and guidance on when to use one, the other or both.

Section 2 presents the SPP as a self-delimited carrier whose only addressing feature is the Application Process Identifier (APID). It stresses that the SPP defines no routing or network service: packets flow along *managed data paths* configured by management, and the APID naming domain (usually one spacecraft) is allocated by the project. The service is preconfigured, one-way, asynchronous, unconfirmed, incomplete and not sequence-preserving. A worked example shows an instrument that uses three managed data paths: images to the ground, commands to the instrument and status back to the control system, with store-and-forward handled transparently.

Section 3 describes the EPP as a 'shim' that carries protocol data units (PDUs) without an authorised Packet Version Number over the Space Data Link Protocols (TM, TC, AOS, Proximity-1, USLP). The Encapsulated Protocol Identifier, registered in SANA, identifies the user. An example shows CFDP over EPP.

Section 4 is a FAQ. It covers layering, coexistence with IP and DTN (IP over CCSDS), reliability (COP-1, COP-P, CFDP, LTP or the application itself), real-time traffic (priority Virtual Channels, the AOS/USLP Insert Zone), segmentation of large data with the Sequence Flags, extending the APID domain through the secondary header, and the SPP versus EPP trade-off: header size, ancillary data and maximum length.

key_points.text: The Report defines both the SPP and the EPP as protocols that are 'not a Network Layer protocol'; the SPP can act as an Application Layer protocol or as a 'shim' between upper-layer protocols and the Space Data Link Layer.

The SPP defines no path, network or routing functionality; aside from the APID it defines none of the mechanisms of a managed data path, which is configured by design or by a management system before data transfer.

APIDs are unique only within one naming domain, which usually corresponds to a spacecraft; the space project that owns the domain allocates the APIDs. CCSDS defines no standard APID domain naming service; missions sub-allocate the domain or extend it with mission-specific secondary-header fields.
SPP services are preconfigured, unidirectional, asynchronous, unconfirmed, incomplete and non-sequence-preserving; two-way exchanges need two managed data paths, one per direction.
The SPP gives no delivery confirmation and no retransmission; reliability is left to the user application or to higher-layer protocols such as LTP or CFDP, or to the Data Link Layer.

The nominal example uses three managed data paths for one instrument: preprocessed images to the ground analysis system, commands from the ground to the instrument, and periodic status back to the control system.
The main purpose of the EPP is to carry PDUs that have no authorised Packet Version Number over the Space Data Link Protocols, using their VC, MAP or Proximity-1 Packet Services.

The EPP carries exactly one user data unit per Encapsulation Packet, unchanged; the maximum data unit length is 4,294,967,287 octets. Unlike the SPP service, the EPP service is sequence-preserving, and the provider may signal gaps.
An EPP user is identified by the Encapsulated Protocol Identifier (EPI), registered in SANA; a SAP is the combination of a PVN, an EPI and an SDLP channel.
IP over CCSDS (CCSDS 702.1-B-1) carries IP PDUs one-for-one in Encapsulation Packets, using the Internet Protocol Extension (IPE) convention.
Point-to-point reliability for packets can come from COP-1 (telecommand frames) or COP-P (Proximity-1 frames); isochronous data can use the Insert Zone of AOS or USLP.

The maximum Space Packet is 65536 octets; larger data units are segmented by the source application, and the primary-header Sequence Flags mark the first and last segments, with the secondary header available for a segment number.

Trade-off: the Encapsulation Packet header is configurable from 1 to 8 octets against the fixed 6-octet Space Packet primary header, but it has no field for ancillary data such as time or for extending the naming domain.

notes: PDF pages 1 and 2 are identical cover pages; the extraction shows 29 PDF pages (registry: 28), the last one blank. The running header reads 'CCSDS Report Concerning the Packet Protocols', slightly different from the cover title 'Space Packet Protocols'. All 18 entries of 1.5 are plain references (an informational report has no normative references); four are SANA registry web pages. Reference [7] cites USLP Issue 2 (732.1-B-2, October 2021); the library holds the newer Issue 3 (ccsds-732-1-732x1b3e1). It is a companion to the library items ccsds-133-0-133x0b2e2 (SPP) and ccsds-133-1-133x1b3e1 (EPP), and complements the stack overview ccsds-130-0-130x0g4e1 and the data link rationale ccsds-130-2-130x2g3. The figures (protocol stack, example configuration, CFDP over EPP) are text-extracted only as labels. No individual authors are named. The Secretariat e-mail address on PDF p. 3 is not reproduced.
